specPoints.text: explain Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection

primer.text: Evolution has a mechanism, and Darwin named it. This note sets out the two-part theory and then drills the four-step selection recipe — variation, survival, reproduction, rising allele frequency — through two exam favourites, snail shell colour and the peppered moth, so you can transfer the recipe to any unfamiliar example an examiner invents.

lessons.title: Darwin's Two Claims and the Selection Recipe
sourceHeadings: Darwin's Theory of Evolution by Natural Selection
lessons.opening: Darwin's account pairs two claims: species have changed over evolutionary time, and natural selection is the mechanism driving that change, as individuals whose genes suit their environment survive longer, reproduce more and leave more of their alleles behind.
keyPoints: Individuals within a species vary, and the variation is rooted in their genes.
Characteristics suited to the environment raise an individual's chance of surviving.
Survivors reproduce more, passing on their advantageous alleles.
Across many generations the advantageous characteristics grow more common.
The pattern earned the label survival of the fittest.

low.restatement: Individuals that fit their surroundings live longer and breed more, so their traits spread.
low.analogy: A sieve shaking soil: the grains that fit the mesh stay on top and dominate what remains.
low.examPointer: Learn the four steps in order; exam marks follow the sequence.

medium.restatement: Selection changes allele frequencies across generations rather than changing any individual during its life.
medium.analogy: Populations drift like drip-filled buckets: each generation adds its drop to the frequency.
medium.examPointer: Never write that individuals evolve; populations do, generation by generation.

check.stem: What two claims make up Darwin's theory as taught here?

options.text: Evolutionary change has happened, and natural selection drove it
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The first claim states that change has occurred.

options.text: Change is working towards a goal
options.explanation: Selection has no destination or purpose.
Survival differences are the engine of the theory.

check.stem: What causes the variation on which selection acts?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Effort cannot rewrite the genes an individual was born with.
Populations do not adapt by wishing.
The environment selects; the genes supply the raw variation.

check.stem: Why are better-suited individuals described as fitter?

options.text: They survive longer and reproduce more successfully
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Fitness means reproductive success, not muscle.
Size is not the measure of fitness.

options.text: They avoid reproducing to stay safe
options.explanation: Fitness is measured through offspring.

check.stem: What happens to advantageous alleles across generations?

options.text: They become more common in the population
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Successful alleles are inherited onwards.

options.text: They stay at the same frequency
options.explanation: The frequency rises, that is the point of selection.
Alleles exist already; need does not summon them.

check.stem: A new predator arrives and only the fastest members of a prey species escape. What follows over generations?

options.text: Speed-related alleles spread because fast individuals survive and breed more
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Everyone runs faster by trying harder
options.explanation: Lifelong effort does not rewrite genes.

options.text: Speed stops mattering once predators settle
options.explanation: The selection pressure keeps acting.
The taught chain follows the prey population's alleles.

check.stem: State the four steps of natural selection in order.
check.modelAnswer: Genetic variation exists, advantageous characteristics raise survival, survivors reproduce and pass on their alleles, and those alleles become more common over generations.

check.stem: Name the scientist and the process he proposed.
check.modelAnswer: Charles Darwin proposed evolution by natural selection.

check.stem: Explain why an advantageous characteristic becomes more common rather than appearing instantly everywhere.
check.modelAnswer: The characteristic starts in a few individuals whose genes carry it; they out-survive and out-reproduce others, so the allele frequency climbs gradually across generations.

check.stem: A population of beetles colonises a windy island where only anchored individuals avoid being blown out to sea. Describe what natural selection does over the following generations.
check.modelAnswer: The anchored individuals survive the wind, breed more successfully than the rest, and their anchoring-related alleles become more common until most of the population carries them.

lessons.title: Selection in Action: Snail Shell Colour
sourceHeadings: Examples of evolution by natural selection
lessons.opening: The selection recipe applies to any trait an examiner invents, and shell colour in snails is a standard worked case: whatever colour matches the surroundings best is eaten less, breeds more and shapes the population over time.
keyPoints: Snail populations carry shell colours that differ between individuals.
A colour that blends with the background suffers less predation.
Better-camouflaged snails survive to reproduce and hand on their colour alleles.
The advantageous colour therefore rises in frequency over generations.

low.restatement: Hidden snails get eaten less, so their shell colour spreads.
low.analogy: Wearing wall-coloured clothing in a game of hide and seek against a hungry seeker.
low.examPointer: Apply the four steps explicitly, naming variation first.

medium.restatement: Predation is the selecting pressure, and the allele for the matching colour gains frequency each generation.
medium.analogy: A background that launders the population towards its own shade.
medium.examPointer: Credit the initial variation to genes, including mutation, before any selection.

check.stem: In the snail example, which snails are eaten less often?

options.text: Those whose shells match the background colour
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Bright shells stand out to predators.
Size is not the taught variable here.
Age does not protect against predation.

check.stem: What direct benefit does better camouflage provide?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Camouflage does not enlarge anything.
The benefit is survival, not speed.
Mutation rates are unaffected by colour.

check.stem: If the environment darkens, what happens to the shell-colour frequencies?

options.text: The darker shells grow more common through selection
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Individuals cannot repaint themselves; frequencies shift through survival.
Selection responds to the changed background.
The advantage follows the background.

check.stem: Where does the initial colour variation among snails come from?

options.text: Genetic differences, including mutations, already present in the population
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Predators select; they do not generate variation.
Shell colour is inherited, not chosen.
The variation is genetic in origin.

check.stem: What must an unfamiliar exam example of natural selection always include?

options.text: Variation, survival differences, reproduction of the advantaged, and rising allele frequency
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Only the name of the species
options.explanation: Naming the organism is not the mechanism.

options.text: A claim that individuals changed themselves
options.explanation: Individuals do not evolve in their lifetimes.

options.text: Proof that humans did the breeding
options.explanation: Natural selection needs no human breeder.

check.stem: Apply the selection steps to an unfamiliar trait, naming each stage.
check.modelAnswer: State the genetic variation, identify which variant survives better, explain that survivors reproduce and pass on their alleles, and conclude the allele becomes more common.

check.stem: Name the advantage held by a matching shell colour.
check.modelAnswer: The matching colour reduces predation, so those snails survive longer.

check.stem: Explain why the snail example is described as natural rather than artificial selection.
check.modelAnswer: No human chooses which snails breed; the environment and predators do the selecting, so survival differences arise naturally rather than from deliberate breeding.

check.stem: A gardener notices that slugs eat mainly the smooth-leafed lettuces and leave the waxy-leafed ones alone. Predict how the lettuce population changes over several seasons without human intervention.
check.modelAnswer: The waxy-leafed plants suffer less predation, so they survive and set more seed, and the wax-related alleles become more common in the lettuce population each season.

lessons.title: Selection in Action: the Peppered Moth
lessons.opening: The peppered moth shows the same logic against an industrial backdrop: birds spot and eat whichever wing colour stands out against soot-darkened or clean bark, so the hidden colour wins each era and its allele spreads.
keyPoints: Moths carry light and dark wing-colour variants in their populations.
On soot-covered bark, dark moths are hidden and light moths stand out.
The better-hidden variant is eaten less and reproduces more.
When bark lightens again, selection reverses and the pale form recovers.

low.restatement: Whichever moth colour matches the bark gets eaten less and becomes more common.
low.analogy: A background that keeps switching sides, promoting whichever player it currently hides.
low.examPointer: Note that selection can reverse; the advantage tracks the environment.

medium.restatement: Predation converts wing colour into survival, and survival into allele frequency changes across generations.
medium.analogy: A see-saw where the environment's weight decides which allele rises.
medium.examPointer: If the question says the bark cleaned up, expect the pale allele to rise.

check.stem: On soot-darkened tree bark, which moths do birds catch more easily?

options.text: The pale forms that stand out
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Dark wings blend into sooty bark.
Camouflage differs between the colour variants.
Birds prey on the conspicuous variant.

check.stem: What role do the birds play in the story?

options.text: They act as the selecting pressure through predation
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Mutation is random and internal to the moths.
No artificial breeding occurs.

options.text: They are irrelevant to the outcome
options.explanation: Predation is precisely the selection pressure.

check.stem: What would happen to allele frequencies if the bark cleaned up?

options.text: The pale variant would regain the advantage and rise
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The dark form keeps rising forever
options.explanation: Selection follows the background, which has changed.
The population keeps both alleles while frequencies shift.
Reversal is the taught outcome.

check.stem: Do individual moths change their wing colour during their lifetime?

options.text: No, selection shifts which colour variants are more common
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Wing colour is fixed at the individual level.
The variants are genetic, not dietary.
Each moth carries its inherited colour.

check.stem: Which statement ties the peppered moth to Darwin's selection mechanism?

options.text: Predation differentiates survival, so the better-camouflaged allele spreads across generations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Predation selects; it does not raise mutation.
Learning plays no part in wing colour.
The alleles belong to the moths.

check.stem: Describe how the peppered moth population changes when soot covers the bark.
check.modelAnswer: Birds eat more of the conspicuous pale moths, so the dark, better-camouflaged individuals survive and breed, and the dark allele becomes more common.

check.stem: Name the two wing-colour variants carried by the moth population.
check.modelAnswer: Light and dark wing-colour variants are present in the population.

check.stem: Explain why both colour variants can persist in the population before selection shifts.
check.modelAnswer: Each variant survives somewhere between clean and sooty backgrounds, so neither allele is eliminated outright, and both remain available for selection to favour.

check.stem: A factory closes and the air over the woodland clears over twenty years. Describe the expected change in the moth population's wing colours.
check.modelAnswer: With clean bark the pale moths are better hidden, so they are eaten less, breed more, and the pale allele rises in frequency while the dark form declines.

glossary.definition: The process in which better-suited individuals survive and breed more, spreading their alleles.
The label given to natural selection, where fitness means surviving to reproduce.
A gene version that improves survival or reproduction in the current environment.
Colouring that hides an organism against its background, reducing predation.
